title: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

sections.title: Distance Between Two Points in the 2-D Plane

slides.title: Streets were coordinates
slides.kicker: A whole city built on a grid — 5000 years ago
bullets: A coordinate system is a structured framework, like grid lines on a map, that uses numbers to describe exact locations.
In the Sindhu-Sarasvati Civilisation, city streets ran precisely North-South and East-West, at uniform distances of about 10 metres.
A merchant could find any shop by counting East-West and North-South units from the city centre — coordinates in daily practice.
slides.note: Grid soch humare yahan bahut purani hai!

slides.title: Baudhayana laid the base
bullets: Baudhayana (c. 800 BCE) used East-West and North-South lines for his deep geometric constructions.
He developed the Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem, laying the foundation of coordinate geometry.
Putting coordinates on the Earth later became vital for navigation across oceans.

slides.title: Zero makes quadrants possible
slides.kicker: Why Brahmagupta matters to this chapter
bullets: Ujjayini was the central longitude meridian from which locations were measured, named 'Arin' in Arabic geography.
Aryabhata (c. 499 CE) replaced Greek 'chords' with 'sines', making star and city coordinates far easier to calculate.
Brahmagupta (c. 628 CE) formalised zero and negative numbers — the 'origin' is zero and negative axes hold values less than zero.

slides.title: Reiaan's felt map
slides.kicker: A blind student 'sees' a room through a grid
bullets: Reiaan moved to a new city; his sister Shalini used coordinate geometry from Grade 9 to help him settle in.
She fixed pins and threads on a rectangular grid to show the floor of the room, using a scale of 1 cm : 1 foot.
Corners of objects were connected with thick wool so Reiaan could feel their positions with his fingers.

slides.title: Why windows are missing
slides.kicker: A map of the floor cannot hold height
bullets: Shalini's sketch only shows the map of the floor — a 2-D picture of a 3-D room.
The position of windows cannot be marked on this map because windows sit at a height above the floor.
A floor map records two directions; height would need a third coordinate.

slides.title: Scale: the quiet hero
slides.kicker: 1 cm on paper = 1 foot in the room
bullets: Every map needs a scale — here 1 cm on the grid stands for 1 foot in the actual room.
With a fixed scale, counting grid units gives real distances a blind learner can trust.
Changing the scale changes every measured distance, so it must stay fixed.

slides.title: One line is not enough
bullets: In earlier grades you used the number line, which is one-dimensional — one number fixes a point.
A 2-D coordinate system uses two lines at right angles to mark points in 2-D space.
The horizontal line is the x-axis; the vertical line is the y-axis; together they are the coordinate axes.

slides.title: The origin O
bullets: The point where the x-axis and y-axis intersect is the origin O, with coordinates (0, 0).
Distances from O are marked in equal units on both axes.
Right of O and upwards from O are positive; left of O and downwards are negative.

slides.title: Reading a point (x, y)
slides.kicker: First x, then y — always in order
bullets: A point's coordinates are written as an ordered pair (x, y): x tells the horizontal move, y the vertical move.
Point H = (0, 4) sits on the y-axis: no horizontal shift, 4 units up.
Point E = (-2.9, 0) sits on the x-axis: 2.9 units left, no vertical shift.

slides.title: Distance when it's slanted
slides.kicker: Axis-parallel was easy — now the diagonal
bullets: If a segment is parallel to an axis, the distance is a simple subtraction of coordinates.
For slanted segments we use the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem, studied in Grade 8.
The horizontal and vertical gaps become the two perpendicular sides of a right triangle.

slides.title: The distance formula
bullets: For points A(x1, y1) and B(x2, y2), the horizontal gap is x2 - x1 and the vertical gap is y2 - y1.
The distance AB = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2) — the hypotenuse of the right triangle.
Squaring removes sign worries: left or right, the gap length is positive.

slides.title: Check with a right angle
slides.kicker: A quick sanity test before you compute
bullets: If two points share an x-coordinate or a y-coordinate, the segment is axis-parallel — subtract directly.
If both coordinates differ, draw the right triangle first, then apply the formula.
The formula never gives a negative distance; if you get one, recheck the squaring.

flashcards.back: A structured framework, like grid lines on a map, that uses numbers to describe the exact location of points or objects.

flashcards.front: Which ancient civilisation built streets on a precise grid about 10 m apart?
flashcards.back: The Sindhu-Sarasvati Civilisation — streets ran exactly North-South and East-West at uniform distances of about 10 metres.

flashcards.front: Which theorem did Baudhayana develop that coordinate geometry stands on?
flashcards.back: The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem, from his constructions with East-West and North-South lines.

flashcards.front: Which city was the zero-longitude meridian in early Siddhantas?
flashcards.back: Ujjayini — it entered Arabic geography as 'Arin', the reference meridian for early maps.

flashcards.front: What did Aryabhata replace 'chords' with, and why?
flashcards.back: He replaced chords with sines (c. 499 CE), making it much easier to calculate coordinates of stars and cities.

flashcards.front: Why is Brahmagupta's work essential for the four-quadrant plane?
flashcards.back: He formalised zero and negative numbers — the origin is zero and negative axes represent values below zero.

flashcards.front: In Shalini's grid model, what scale did she use?
flashcards.back: 1 cm on the grid stood for 1 foot in the actual room (1 cm : 1 foot).

flashcards.front: Why can't windows be marked on Reiaan's floor map?
flashcards.back: The map shows only the floor in 2-D; windows sit at a height above the floor, which needs a third coordinate.

flashcards.front: How did Reiaan 'feel' object positions on the grid?
flashcards.back: Corners of objects were connected with thick wool between pins, so he could trace their positions with his fingers.
The horizontal line through O is the x-axis; the vertical line is the y-axis; they meet at right angles.

flashcards.front: What are the coordinates of the origin?
flashcards.back: The origin O is the intersection of the axes and has coordinates (0, 0).

flashcards.front: Which directions from O are positive?
flashcards.back: Right of O along the x-axis and upwards along the y-axis are positive; left and downwards are negative.
On the y-axis, 4 units above O — x is 0, so there is no horizontal shift.

flashcards.front: How do you find distance between points on a line parallel to the x-axis?
flashcards.back: Subtract their x-coordinates (same y), and take the absolute value of the difference.

flashcards.front: State the distance formula for A(x1, y1) and B(x2, y2).
flashcards.back: AB = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2), from the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem.

flashcards.front: Why can the distance formula never output a negative number?
flashcards.back: Both gaps are squared before adding, so the sum is non-negative and its square root is non-negative.

quiz.q: In the Sindhu-Sarasvati cities, how far apart were the parallel streets?
quiz.why: Streets ran N-S and E-W at uniform distances of about 10 metres.
Baudhayana (c. 800 BCE) used grid lines for deep geometric constructions and developed the theorem.

quiz.q: Why was Brahmagupta's formalisation of zero and negatives crucial for the Cartesian plane?
options: It gave names to the axes
The origin is zero and negative axes need negative numbers
quiz.why: Without zero and negatives as algebraic entities, the four-quadrant plane is impossible.

quiz.q: Shalini's scale is 1 cm : 1 foot. A table is 5 cm across on the grid. How wide is it really?
quiz.why: Each cm stands for one foot, so 5 cm means 5 feet.

quiz.q: Why can't the window's position appear on the floor map?
options: The map is 2-D and windows sit at a height
quiz.why: A floor map records two directions; height would need a third coordinate.

quiz.q: What did the thick wool between pins represent?
quiz.why: Points marking corners of objects were connected with thick wool so their edges could be felt.

quiz.q: The point where the x-axis and y-axis meet is called the
quiz.why: The intersection point of the axes is the origin O with coordinates (0, 0).

quiz.q: A point has coordinates (-3, 2). Where does it sit relative to O?
quiz.why: Negative x means left of O; positive y means upwards.

quiz.q: Which point lies ON the x-axis?
quiz.why: E = (-2.9, 0) has y = 0, so it sits on the x-axis; (0,0) is the origin itself.

quiz.why: The horizontal and vertical gaps form a right triangle; the formula is Pythagoras in coordinates.

examples.title: Locating the study table
examples.problem: On Shalini's room grid (1 cm : 1 foot), the table's corner pin is at (4, 3) from the door pin at O. How far east and how far north is the table corner?
steps: Read the ordered pair (4, 3): x = 4, y = 3.
x = 4 means 4 grid units east — at 1 cm : 1 foot, that is 4 feet east.
y = 3 means 3 grid units north — 3 feet north.
examples.answer: 4 feet east and 3 feet north of the door.

examples.title: Distance across the room
examples.problem: Two pins are at A(1, 2) and B(4, 6) on the grid. Find the straight-line distance between them.
steps: By the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem: AB = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(25).
examples.answer: AB = 5 units (5 feet on the room's scale).
